say.text: Patient A: 58-year-old man, sudden epigastric pain three hours ago. Board-like rigidity, BP 82/50, pulse 122.
The erect film shows free gas under the diaphragm. The diagnosis is clear. What is your first step?

choices.label: Book theatre now; the fluids can run there
IV access, crystalloids and a nasogastric tube
CT abdomen first, to confirm the site
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Surgery is the cure, so it feels like the urgent step.
But surgery is the standard treatment for this picture, not the first step at a pressure of 82 systolic. He must survive the anaesthetic first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: the operation is the cure, but a shocked patient has to be kept alive until it.

say.text: That choice is not right. A scan feels careful, and it would confirm where the hole is.
But a scan does nothing for a falling pressure. A patient in shock is stabilised before any scan or theatre, and bloods guide the fluids.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the order: shock first, then the rest.

say.text: Ask what keeps his pressure up until he reaches the anaesthetist, and what he needs before he is safe to anaesthetise.
Yes. In a shocked patient the first steps keep him alive until theatre: fluids, a nasogastric tube, a catheter and analgesia.
Surgery is still the standard treatment, but it waits for that resuscitation.
Here is patient A worked. Step 1: IV access, crystalloids, nasogastric tube and catheter, started at once.
Step 2: bloods, including group and save, which guide the resuscitation. Patient B shows what comes after that.

choices.label: Next: patient B, last step yours
I know the order, skip to the operation

say.text: Patient B: the same ulcer and the same pressure. Fluids and the nasogastric tube are running, and bloods are sent.
What comes next, before theatre?

choices.label: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and an IV PPI
Omental patch and lavage in theatre, then antibiotics
Consent and shift to theatre; antibiotics can follow
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Definitive repair feels like the real treatment, so it is tempting to put it first.
But repair is the standard operation, not the first move. Antibiotics and a PPI are started on diagnosis, before the patient reaches theatre.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the clock: the drugs start on diagnosis, the operation later.

say.text: That choice is not right. Getting to theatre fast feels urgent, and the antibiotics look like a detail for later.
But they are started as soon as the diagnosis is made, while the fluids run, not after the abdomen is open.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again at when the antibiotics start.

say.text: Bacteria are now spreading into the peritoneal fluid. What is started on diagnosis, before any operation?
Yes. Broad-spectrum antibiotics and an IV PPI start as soon as the diagnosis is made.
Surgery still follows, and it is the standard treatment once he is resuscitated.
Patient C is stable after fluids and antibiotics. The anterior duodenal ulcer has perforated and is still a simple, uncomplicated hole.
Which operation is the standard one?

choices.label: Truncal vagotomy with pyloroplasty and repair
Omental patch closure with peritoneal lavage
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Older exam books pair acid surgery with every ulcer operation, so vagotomy feels like part of the job.
But acid-reducing surgery is no longer routine in the PPI and H. pylori era, and the recurrence is now prevented by treating the cause.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the current frame: acid surgery is no longer added to the repair.

say.text: That choice is not right. A gastrectomy removes the acid source, so it looks like the thorough answer.
But PYQs have offered resection as a distractor, while current practice closes the perforation simply, without resecting the stomach.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what the exam offered against current practice.

say.text: The question asks for the operation that closes the hole. Ask whether it has to change the stomach or the acid supply to do that.
Yes. Simple closure with an omental patch and peritoneal lavage is the standard operation.
After repair, H. pylori eradication and a PPI prevent recurrence. Routine acid-reducing surgery is no longer needed.
The exam keys 'Graham's patch' for a perforated duodenal ulcer. A student asks which statement about the two omental techniques is strictly right.

choices.label: Graham used a free omental plug; Cellan-Jones a pedicled tongue
Graham and Cellan-Jones are two names for one free patch
Graham used a pedicled tongue; Cellan-Jones a free plug
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. The exam gives one name, so it is tempting to think the strict name must be the same patch.
But the two techniques differ in the tissue used: a free plug in one, a pedicled tongue in the other. The exam still accepts either name.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the exam name from the technique.

say.text: That choice is not right. Both techniques use omentum, so the two labels are easy to swap.
But the labels follow the tissue used. Check which technique moves a free piece of omentum and which keeps a pedicled tongue attached.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which tissue each name attaches to.

say.text: The exam name and the tissue are two different things. Ask which technique moves a free piece of omentum and which keeps a tongue attached.
Yes. Graham's patch is a free omental plug; the pedicled tongue of omentum is the Cellan-Jones repair.
PYQs expected 'Graham's patch', and either name scores as omental patch closure in the exam.
Patient E is stable 14 hours after onset, with mild pain and no peritonitis. The surgeon proposes Taylor's conservative method.
What must be shown before that is safe?

choices.label: A barium study to show whether the leak has sealed
Nothing more; he is stable, so Taylor can start now
A water-soluble contrast study showing the leak is sealed
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Barium is the familiar gut contrast, so it is tempting to reach for it here.
But barium is contraindicated when perforation is suspected, because a leak causes severe barium peritonitis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the contrast does if it leaks into the peritoneum.

say.text: That choice is not right. A calm, stable patient looks like one who can simply be watched.
But Taylor's method is reserved for a sealed perforation, and the seal must be shown on contrast before conservative care starts.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifier: sealed and shown on contrast.

say.text: Taylor needs proof that the hole is walled off. Which study shows that without the risk of a leak into the peritoneum?
Yes. Taylor's method is for a sealed perforation, and the seal is shown by a water-soluble contrast study.
Conservative care is then nasogastric suction, fluids, antibiotics and a PPI.

choices.label: Go deeper: when does conservative care fail?

say.text: Conservative care is unsuitable for the elderly, and for anyone not improving within about 12 to 24 hours, who then need surgery.
Elderly man on steroids. Free gas on the erect film, generalised peritonitis, pulse 120, BP 100/64 after fluids.
What is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: Taylor management, since his pressure is holding on fluids
Resuscitate, then omental patch closure and lavage
Taylor management, since the diagnosis is already made
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. Holding a pressure on fluids looks like stability, and stability is what Taylor asks for.
But Taylor is for a sealed perforation shown on contrast. Free gas with generalised peritonitis is a surgical problem.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifier: sealed, not just stable.

say.text: That choice is not right. Once the diagnosis is made, conservative care can seem a reasonable next step.
But a diagnosis is not a seal. Taylor needs a contained leak shown on contrast, and this abdomen has spread contamination.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate knowing the perforation from knowing it is sealed.

say.text: Ask first whether this abdomen holds a walled-off leak or free contamination. Then ask what the patient needs before theatre.
Yes. Free perforation with generalised peritonitis is surgical, and the patient is resuscitated while theatre is prepared.
The operation is an omental patch closure with peritoneal lavage.
The Boey score predicts mortality from three items: shock on admission, major coexisting illness, and delay to surgery.
Which pair of thresholds is correct for the shock and the delay items?

choices.label: Systolic below 90 mmHg, and delay over 24 hours
Systolic below 100 mmHg, and delay over 12 hours
Systolic below 100 mmHg, and delay over 24 hours
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. A systolic of 90 feels like the line for shock, because it is used in other scores.
But the 90 mmHg line is not the Boey cut-off. Mortality rises with shock, and the score uses its own threshold.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the Boey shock threshold against the other scores you know.

say.text: That choice is not right. Twelve hours sounds like a sensible delay, since early surgery matters.
But 12 hours is not the Boey delay item. The score counts delay beyond a longer interval.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the delay item in the score.

say.text: Recall the three items: shock, comorbidity and delay. Which thresholds belong to the first and the third?
Yes. Boey uses shock on admission (systolic below 100 mmHg), major coexisting illness, and delay to surgery over 24 hours.
Age raises mortality, but it is not one of the three Boey items.
Patient H: 62 years old, weight loss over two months. A perforated gastric ulcer is closed with an omental patch and washed out.
What is still missing?

choices.label: Nothing; the patch and lavage complete the repair
Biopsy or excision of the ulcer edge
Truncal vagotomy at the same sitting, for acid
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right. A duodenal ulcer is closed this way, so the same pathway feels complete.
But a perforated gastric ulcer can be a carcinoma, which the duodenal pathway never checks. Weight loss is the cue here.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the stomach can hide that the duodenum does not.

say.text: That choice is not right. Acid causes ulcers, so cutting acid at the same sitting feels thorough.
But acid-reducing surgery is no longer routine in the PPI and H. pylori era, and it does nothing about a possible carcinoma.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what the modern repair adds, and what it leaves out.

say.text: Ask what this ulcer might be, apart from an ulcer, in a 62-year-old who is losing weight.
Yes. A perforated gastric ulcer must be biopsied or excised, because it may be a perforated carcinoma.
The patch closure is still the operation; the biopsy is the extra step that the duodenal pathway lacks.
The order: resuscitate first, then antibiotics and a PPI, then the omental patch with lavage.
Taylor is only for a sealed perforation on a water-soluble study. A gastric ulcer is biopsied, and routine vagotomy is not part of the repair.
Antibiotics and an IV PPI start on diagnosis, because bacteria are already spreading. They run while he is resuscitated, before theatre.
Taylor is for a sealed perforation shown on contrast. Free gas with generalised peritonitis is spreading contamination, so he is resuscitated and then repaired.
